text: Knowing when an LLM is wrong: uncertainty estimation methods, and the LM-Polygraph library
Ahmad Bin Qasim
Problem: Confidently wrong
Confidently wrong
A wrong answer arrives with the same certainty as a right one.
Four of the 7B model's BioASQ answers. Each is wrong against the reference, and each got a probability above 0.98 from the model itself. Nothing in the text of an answer says which ones to check.
What an uncertainty score is for
Rank the answers, flag the least certain, and what is kept gets better.

Accuracy of the answers kept as the most uncertain are flagged for review, ranked by mean token entropy. Flagging half of them lifts the kept accuracy from 45% to 67%. A useless score stays on the flat line; a perfect one follows the upper dashed line. AUROC, used in the results, measures how well the ranking separates right from wrong.
Methods: Where the uncertainty is
Where a method looks for doubt
Two questions place every method: what you can see of the model, and how many answers you draw.

Further right needs more access: a hosted API gives only text, an open model also gives token probabilities and hidden states. Lower down, the same question is sampled several times. The next slides take each family in turn.
Five places to look for doubt
Every estimator reads one of five signals, and each needs different access to the model.

White-box needs the model's probabilities or internals; black-box needs only its text. Families and method names follow Vazhentsev et al. (arXiv:2605.14570); self-report is added here because p(True) is in the run. T1–T4 are the tiers the results are grouped by.
Reading the probabilities
One forward pass, and the model has already said how sure it was.
All three come out of the pass that produced the answer, so they need nothing beyond generation. They need the token probabilities, which many hosted APIs do not return.
Asking the model
A second prompt asks the model to judge its own answer.
p(True) reads the probability the model puts on “True”; the empirical variant samples the verdict ten times and counts. Both need one more prompt per answer, which is tier 2.
Asking again
If repeated samples disagree, the first answer was a guess.

Sample several answers to the same question and measure how far they agree: by shared words, or by meaning, with an NLI model testing whether two answers entail each other. Sampling is tier 3; the NLI model on top is tier 4. White-box variants also weight each sample by its probability.
Training a detector
A classifier on the model's hidden states can learn what a wrong answer looks like — given labels.
Probes need graded answers from the task they will be used on, and a new set for every new task or model. They are named here for completeness and were not run.
Tooling: LM-Polygraph
LM-Polygraph
One library runs every one of these estimators behind one interface.
Open source, pip-installable. An estimator returns one uncertainty score per answer, higher meaning less sure; grading the answers and scoring the estimators against them is a separate step.
What is in the library
Thirty-eight methods, filed under five categories, with the plumbing to compare them.

Categories and counts are LM-Polygraph's own, from its README; the grey note on each bar is the closest family on the methods slides. Density-based and ensembling methods need training data or several models, which is why the talk does not run them.
Tooling: Your model, your data
Wrapping a model
Wrap the model once, then score any answer with any estimator.

WhiteboxModel takes a Hugging Face model and tokenizer; BlackboxModel takes an API, which limits you to black-box estimators unless it returns log-probabilities. Eager attention is required on transformers 5.x. The left block was run as shown; its output is underneath.
UEManager: a whole dataset at once
One object runs every estimator over a dataset and scores how well each ranks the answers.

Each answer gets a quality from the generation metric and a score from every estimator; the UE metric then asks how well each estimator's ranking follows the quality. The BioASQ study in this talk is this call with 20 estimators and its own grader.
Adding your own estimator
A new method is a class with three parts, and it plugs into everything above.
This one scores an answer by its least likely token. It ran inside UEManager alongside the built-in estimators, sharing their statistics.
Example: A small BioASQ study
The benchmark: BioASQ factoids
1,000 short biomedical questions, each with a short reference answer.

Questions from the BioASQ challenges, kept only where a reference answer is at most five words, so right and wrong can be told apart. Answers are graded by exact match, then by token rules, then by manual labels for what no rule can settle. Those labels were proposed with LLM help and checked, not set by domain experts.
Every estimator, by type and tier
Types say what signal a method reads; tiers, what it needs to run.

Every estimator in the results, placed by signal type and tier. Tiers are cumulative: each adds one requirement to the one before. Sampling methods split across tiers 3 and 4 by whether they also need the NLI model.
Example: What it showed
Every estimator, ranked
Tier 1 holds both the winner and the traps.

AUROC for separating wrong answers from right ones, with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. Blue is tier 1 — one forward pass, no sampling and no second model. Hollow markers are sign-inverted: they return a confidence rather than an uncertainty, and read as 1−AUROC.
What each tier adds
Sampling and an NLI model add consistency, not a higher ceiling.

Each dot is one estimator, placed in its tier; the bar is the tier median. Tiers are cumulative: each column adds one requirement to the one before — a second prompt, then sampling, then a DeBERTa NLI model over the sample set.
Conclusions and outlook
What this is, and what it is not
An introduction, not a benchmark: your mileage may vary.
Treat the ranking as a starting point. Before relying on an estimator, re-run the comparison on your own task, model and grading; LM-Polygraph makes that a short script.
Take-home
Wrap your model once, score every answer, and check the scores on your own task.
Point three is the one result carried over from the BioASQ example, and the previous slide says how far it travels. The rest holds whatever the task.
References
Where the methods, the library and the data come from.
The key on the left says what each paper backs, in the colour it has on the method slides. The LM-Polygraph README credits a paper for each of its 38 methods.
Backup
The scores behind the AUROC
Tier 1 against tier 4 — the overlap looks much the same.

Raw uncertainty scores for every question, split by whether the answer was graded correct. An AUROC in the high 0.7s still means two heavily overlapping distributions: this is a triage signal, not a verdict.
The same methods on other models
Of the one-pass methods, only mean token entropy holds everywhere.

Each line is one estimator's AUROC across six models from four families: flat means it holds. The ranking mostly transfers (mean pairwise Spearman ρ 0.87). Mean token entropy is the only tier-1 method that stays above 0.75 on all six, between 0.76 and 0.83; max sequence probability and perplexity, read from the same forward pass, fall to around 0.60 on Mistral. A tier-4 method beats mean token entropy significantly on two of the six. All six runs were graded with the full manual label set.
